speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and take part in this important debate on the borrowing authority Bill, Bill C-21. Two days ago, all Members of the House joined in honouring the work done over a period of some 60 years by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who has fought long and hard on behalf of the poor, pensioners and the powerless for a better and more compassionate Canada.
I was pleased to be a part of the group which honoured the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre that day and I think it is important that when we take part in a debate on a Bill as significant as this Bill, which seeks authority to borrow almost $30 billion, we reflect on some of the principles of which the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre spoke during the remarks he made two days ago. I think it is
March 15, 1984

important that we recognize very clearly our responsibilities as the representatives of the people of our constituencies. I think it is important that we not bicker with one another but speak out constructively regarding our options and proposals to deal with what is clearly the most important economic crisis facing the people of the country, and that is the devastating crisis of unemployment.
It is essential that the Government, when seeking the authority to borrow some $30 billion, clearly recognize that its most important priority must be putting back to work the almost two million Canadians who want to work and cannot find jobs. We are not only dealing with the literally hundreds of thousands of people who are in their fifties and early sixties and have been laid off from their jobs or fired or, as a result of technological change, found themselves no longer able to continue with the work they have been doing for many, many years. We must deal as well with a whole generation of young people.
In excess of half a million young people are desperately looking for work but find that the doors are closed, that as a result of the bankruptcy of the Government's economic policies they are unable to work. At the same time, because of the catastrophic economic policies of the Government, we find that access to post-secondary education is becoming more and more restricted. Young people are being hit with a double-whammy. On the one hand, they are unable to find work; on the other, they find that the opportunities for continuing education are becoming more and more restricted as a result of cutbacks in post-secondary education funding.
As well, Mr. Speaker, we find that women and the disabled are affected to a very significant extent by cutbacks. Governments, both federal and provincial, have refused to implement mandatory affirmative action plans to ensure that women are not the first victims on the firing line in these rough economic times.
Many of us are also concerned about the fact that at a time when Canadians are bearing a record level of debt on a per capita basis, the Government refuses to make the necessary changes to the federal income tax system, whether to the corporate income tax structure or to the personal income tax structure, to ensure that loopholes are closed and that large corporations are paying their fair share.
We hear much talk from members of the Official Opposition about the size of the deficit. I share the Opposition's concern about the burgeoning deficit but they are silent when it comes to putting an end to the massive network of the so-called corporate tax expenditures. These expenditures amount, in effect, to direct grants to the corporate sector and in 1979 totalled some $6 billion. We know that the tax system for the banks in this country is effectively a voluntary "pay-as-you-go" system. How on earth can they defend a system in which Revenue Canada puts the boots to ordinary working men and women at the same time as they turn a blind eye to loopholes which permit literally billions of dollars to be retained in corporate coffers instead of being spent on job-creation programs?
Borrowing Authority Act
There are many ways in which we could move forward to create jobs in this country, such as by significantly enhancing research and development. Our record of R and D is one of the worst in the western economic world.
There is a host of other programs which could be implemented immediately to create jobs, whether it be identifying public works projects in conjunction with local municipalities, work that has to be done now and should be done, such as in the forestry sector which has been disgracefully neglected by both federal and provincial governments. As the Science Council of Canada has noted, there is a serious crisis in the industry and if we are not prepared to take emergency steps toward reforestation and conservation of our forest industry, we may lose it. For a Member of Parliament from British Columbia where forestry is the number one industry, that is obviously a very serious matter.
There must be a fundamental restructuring of our economy to strengthen the manufacturing sector. There is no excuse for the fact that Canadians are the largest per capita importers of agricultural and mining machinery in the world. We are quite capable of making our own mining and agricultural machinery and putting Canadians to work in that way. We should have a Canadian merchant marine and ship Canadian goods on Canadian ships.
It is essential that in dealing with the whole question of technological change we must be its masters and not its servants. Where working people are affected by technological change, they should have the right to negotiate and there should be provision to give them ample notice. It is women who are affected to a disproportionate extent by technological change. We must look at the length of the work week, at early retirement, at part-time work for those who want it and at effective retraining schemes for those affected by technological change.
Over the past six or eight months, I have gone out to the doorsteps of my constituency of Burnaby and listened to the people I represent. In my constituency office in south Burnaby my assistant, Del Carrel, and I have noted a dramatic increase in the level of personal hardship and suffering being experienced in that community. I am sure the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) and others from British Columbia have experienced the same thing. We see the devastating impact of the Government's economic policies on the people we represent, whether they be pensioners, young people or those thrown out of work.
What alternative does the Official Opposition offer? Occasionally we get a few hints. The Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) has said: "If I told you what I would do we would never get elected". Just a few weeks ago he told us what the Tories would do with respect to the means test for old age pensioners and for family allowances. He is the official finance spokesperson for the Tory Party. He said:
You have to look and see, on the social side, whether it is possible to introduce more means testing so that programs are not universal,-

That is the vision of the Conservative Party in this country. We have seen the devastating impact of the Liberal Party. Now more than ever it is essential that Canadians listen to the voice of the New Democratic Party, listen to the voice of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre. It is time for a government which puts people ahead of profits.

Mr. Speaker, in the first two presentations made this morning you have heard the voice of profligacy. You heard it from the Liberal Party, desperately trying to defend the proposal to borrow some $30 billion, and you heard the voice of the New Democratic Party-that voice that is getting weaker day by day as people realize what they are up to-saying that a $30 billion deficit is not enough, that we should spend more. If the Liberals are bad, as they are, then the New Democrats are three times worse.
Now you are going to hear the voice of responsibility, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: It is five times worse!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
That is the voice of the Conservative Opposition. We are completely of a contrary mind to the Government when it comes to its request to borrow some $30 billion. We note that even in its own Budget documents tabled in the House, the requirement was only for some $25.5 billion. That is what it told Parliament it needed for the balance of the fiscal year. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that; I think the Government will come back for yet another borrowing authority later, but that is what it said.
When we examine this Bill we see that there is built into it a borrowing authority for $4 billion in excess of what the Government told us it wanted a couple of weeks ago. It is pretty obvious what it is up to: it wants to establish a $4 billion slush fund. We know why it wants that slush fund; it is because an election will be coming up in the not too distant future. I wish we could have it next week and get it over with and have a new government in Canada. I am scared of what might happen if we let these gentlemen go around the country with that $4 billion at election time. In the past we have seen what they do when they have money in their pockets, money with which they are prepared to try to buy votes, money with which to bribe the public of Canada-trying to bribe the public of Canada with its own tax dollars which have been confiscated by the Government.
Let us put this borrowing request into context. This is the eighth time in this Parliament that the Government has made a request to borrow yet more funds. Every time it comes before Parliament with this request it is for more money; it is a roller-coaster request and there seems to be no end to it.
In the Budget documents presented on February 15 the projected financial requirements from the current 1984-85 fiscal year over the next three years to the 1987-88 fiscal year is some $87.25 billion. Even if that estimate is correct it means that within the next three years the Government will come back time and time again with a request for more borrowing
authority. I hope the election is called soon and the Government changes so that we can have a responsible government which will put a responsible financial policy into effect and these requests will not be necessary. Under the present system, the present spending plan of the Government, a steady stream of like Bills is guaranteed. There is no hope for the taxpayers of Canada with the present Government in office.
Let us look, Sir, at the history of the financial mismanagement of the Liberal Party. When did we first get ourselves on this treadmill? I believe it started in the days when John Turner-John "Deficit" Turner, as my friend, the Hon. Member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Clark), called him the other day-was Minister of Finance. Previous to that we had been in a state of balance for some time. Some years there may have been a deficit and some years a surplus, but things would even out. That is the way government should be run. However, Sir, under the ministry of that hon. gentleman, the leading light, the golden boy of the Liberal Party-or so the press would have us believe-deficits were run up of some $5.5 billion.
When that gentleman left office, Sir, in came someone who is presently contending for the leadership of the Liberal Party, a gentleman who presently occupies the position of Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien). As Minister of Finance he, in the Liberal way, went a little further than his predecessor. He ran up a debt of some $12.25 billion during his term of office. After that in came another leading light in the Party opposite, a gentleman who is presently Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). In his term he almost doubled the record of the previous incumbent. He came to Parliament for $25.25 billion. Finally, Sir, in this history of mismanagement we come to the present incumbent in that high office, the gentleman who in one year can run up deficits of $31.5 billion. It gets worse and worse.
John Turner put us on this treadmill and no one yet has been able to get us off. If you examine the sequence I have just outlined, Sir, you will see that in good Liberal tradition that Party alternated between an English-speaking Canadian and a French-speaking Canadian for that ministerial position. I am told this is a tradition with the gentlemen opposite. But this formula, this transition from English to French, at least when applied to Ministers of Finance, appears to be nothing more than a formula for disaster.
I would suspect that were the same to occur in the leadership aspirations of the gentlemen opposite, much the same would occur. That Party has gotten us into such a state now that the accumulated gross national debt at the end of this month, the end of the present fiscal year, will be some $190 billion. This is about half the annual Gross National Product of Canada. This is the situation in which we find ourselves.
Hon. Members on this side of the House have spoken eloquently on what this means to Canada. What it means. Sir, is the destruction of the national economy of Canada; of that there is no doubt. That has been explained on many occasions.

I see that I have very little time left. Suffice it to say that just the costs of servicing this debt are now $20 billion per year. That is about $1 in every $3 raised in the form of taxes from Canadians. The result of this policy of financial mismanagement year after year after year has been the following: a higher burden of taxes on all Canadians; higher interest rates, as the Government has to compete within the capital markets of the country, affecting employment, housing construction and other elements of the economy.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It is an article in the Toronto Sun of February 16. This is the advice it gives to the Government and, I would think, to the Hon. Member for Willowdale:
Borrowing Authority Act
The Liberals have missed their last chance to do something effective. High taxes, high government spending and the resulting inflation have wrecked Canada's economy.
If Lalonde really wanted the private sector to create jobs he should have slashed government spending and cut taxes. Instead he's merely handed out minor sops.
Yet in spite of all the bluster, taxes are going up. The 1 per cent increase in the federal sales tax will result in large across-the-board increases on everything.
This is not leadership-just more jiggery-pokery that's caused our once strong dollar to lose 25 per cent of its value and the Canadian deficit to grow 30 per cent larger in per capita terms than that of the U.S.
How was it done? Simple. By reducing competitiveness through ever-increasing government regulation and interference-
It is just as simple as that. Apparently, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Willowdale is not reading his own local papers. He says we have no policies. That is what we believe in. That is just exactly what we will do when we form the Government.
I am sure Canadians do not realize the amount of money the Government is spending which it does not have. The rapidly increasing expenditures are going to put a burden on future generations which they will never be able to pay off. We are mortgaging the lives of our children and grandchildren. We cannot spend $11,250,000 an hour 24 hours a day every day of the year, Sundays and holidays included. This is a horrendous sum, Mr. Speaker.
The Canadian people must begin to realize the direction in which the Government has been leading them. In my constituency I find that more and more people are starting to think about what is happening. I hear a lot of people talking about the tremendous deficit and the effect it is going to have on the economy, their lives and their livelihood. It cannot be otherwise. The Government is taking too much out of the system and not leaving enough for the business community to survive or expand. That is the engine we must use to get back to where we were in 1968 when the present administration took over.
I would like to bring to the attention of the House some comments made by Mr. W. R. Wyman, who is Chairman of the Board of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. This is his advice as to what the Government should do. This is free advice. It is available to the Government but apparently it does not understand what it reads. He said:
What we need is not nostalgia, nor is it a new crop of trendy slogans touting temporary restraint. We do need a new national commitment to an economic regime that is based on individual freedoms and responsibility, with that individual freedom protected by the right to acquire, hold and use property. And, lest anyone miss the point, it will be impossible to promote that freedom and responsibility unless the distribution of rewards is determined by the free market.
That is where the Government has gone wrong, Mr. Speaker. The Government is not allowing the free market system to make this determination. The Government is making this determination. It is being made by Members such as the Hon. Member for Willowdale who does not understand what it is all about. Mr. Wyman went on to say:
To use an overworked phrase, the "Just Society", based on individual freedoms, cannot prevail if people interfere in the market, and the rush to regulate in

the last two decades has not, on balance, proven its worth to our society. Quite the opposite. It has retarded growth, encouraged inflation, and undermined our competitiveness.
No, the long-term path to progress-to recovery, if you will-lies in Government restraint not just in spending but in overall terms. In its size. In its activities. In its will to guide us from cradle to grave. No thinking person would deny Government's role in formulating economic and social goals for Canada, but I'm suggesting it need not and should not be concerned with specifying the means to achieve those goals. That is better left to the marketplace.
That is sound advice, Mr. Speaker. I do not know where you would get any better. In place of that we have the Minister of Finance saying he is not worrying because the value of the Canadian dollar is depreciating. He is not lying awake at night thinking about that. When the value of the Canadian dollar depreciates the first effect is that we run into inflation. This is devastating. We must be able to control inflation. The only way we will do that is to have more responsibility put into the marketplace in the hands of the Canadian people. The Government must create that climate in order for that to take place. That is the best advice I can give the people opposite. I hope they pay attention.

Mr. Speaker, the Bill we have before us is very light and short. The body of the Bill is contained on one page about eight inches by eleven inches. Even though it is light and very short, that is not the effect it is going to have upon the Canadian people. Its weight -will substantially add to the burden of debt which rests upon 'the shoulders of Canadians today. The effects will span the years and enchain our children and our children's children for generations to come,
I have lost count of the times I have heard Liberal spokesmen declare that their intention was and is to exercise restraint and reduce the deficit. However, like most of the predictions made in so many areas, the announced goals were seldom, if ever, realized. In seeking borrowing authority for the unprecedented amount of $29.55 billion in this Bill before us, the Government has reduced its diminishing credibility to minus zero.
I listened with interest this morning to the speech of the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson). He stated that we in the Progressive Conservative Party have been asking for the impossible in requesting reduced deficits. Why, then, has that been promised so often by the Liberals? Apparently they had no more intention of reducing the deficit and exercising restraint than they had when they promised to keep the price of gasoline lower than that which was predicted by the Conservative Government several years ago.
The Government is asking for authority to borrow $29.55 billion. This is the eighth time the Government has come before this Parliament to request such authority. Bill C-30 was for $12 billion. Bill C-59 was for $14 billion. Bill C- 111 was for $6.6 billion. Bill C-125 was for $7 billion. Bill C-128 was for $4 billion. Bill C-143 was for $19 billion. Bill C-151 was for $10.71 billion. Now, Mr. Speaker, we have the unconscionable Bill C-21 requesting $29.55 billion. This is a total of $102 billion requested in this Parliament.
As has been underlined by several of my colleagues in the course of debate, the amount requested in this Bill is far in excess of the amount required to meet the Government's commitments. There has been no clear reason given why the request has been made or for what purposes the money will be used. The Government's spokespersons, including the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), have loudly declared that economic recovery is the prevailing trend today. I suggest that the evidence points to the contrary. I think it is safe to say that any seeming degree of recovery is, at the very best, exceedingly fragile. Furthermore, unemployment as of January this year stands at 11.2 per cent. Manufacturing is at 70.5 per cent of capacity and business and farming bankruptcies continue at an alarming rate. Farm income is declining. These facts do not indicate or support in any way the claim that recovery is a continuing reality.
I would like to call attention to the report of the Conference Board of January, 1984. It points out that the Canadian economy will experience four quarters of negative growth in 1985. The rate of job creation will slow over the course of 1984 and 1985, and will be negative in the last half of 1984. As a consequence, unemployment will fall to 10.8 per cent this summer and then rise to 11.3 per cent by the end of next year. It points out that the federal deficit is seen as remaining in the $27 billion range on a national accounts basis. Short-term interest rates will rise by two percentage points between now and the end of 1985. Capital investment will continue to be weak or negative. I do not believe there is anything in those figures that would indicate that the recovery is even holding, let alone improving across the country.
I suggest that the Bill in its current form is completely unacceptable. While we can acknowledge the necessity to meet the legitimate costs of a responsible government, we cannot meekly permit the Government to build up a surplus to finance unknown activities at taxpayers' expense.
When we look at the entire picture, I cannot understand how the Government has the colossal nerve to come before this Parliament and ask us to support a measure that will impose such a further horrendous deficit upon the Canadian people and demand that they contribute another $29.5 billion without indicating what it will be used for or how it will affect our country.
If we could see that these vast expenditures were improving the lot of the Canadian people, perhaps it would be entirely different. However, the figures that I and many of my colleagues have presented to the House would indicate that, to the contrary, it is simply a matter of pouring money into a hole in the ground. Rather than seeing an improvement so that our people are happy, contented, prosperous and confident, I believe when people see the activities of the Government and the demands it is making on the taxpayers of this country, they become increasingly depressed, to the point where we find that the social effects upon Canadian society because of the eco-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of speaking to the House this afternoon on Bill C-21. Just in case, Sir, that you are unaware of what this debate is about, it is debate on second reading of a Bill to give authority to the Government to borrow $29.5 billion. This is the largest borrowing Bill in Canada's history.
When you talk about borrowing in the House, that inevitably brings up the question of the deficit. The deficit brings up the general question of taxation, and taxation and all of these other subjects bring up the general topic of the economy of the day. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, it is not easy these days to get people excited about the economy, but it is, nevertheless, the single most important Government issue facing Canadians in general today.
Any way you look at it, Canada is in a deepening financial crisis. I think any doubts about that were rudely dispelled by last month's federal Budget which told us that Canada's deficit-and the borrowing Bill is directly related to that deficit-will be $31.5 billion this year and more than $25 billion for each of the next four years. By the end of the fiscal year 1987-88 the national debt of Canada will climb to $261.5 billion. That is almost four times the 1979-80 level of $68.6 billion. Four times in less than ten years the national debt has grown.
These multibillion dollar figures are almost impossible for me to grasp-I do not know about you, Sir-considering that most of us will never even see a million dollars during our lifetimes. But these horrendous deficits do affect us all directly in ways in which I think we can all easily understand. Basically those deficits, and this borrowing Bill, mean that higher
interest rates for bank loans or for mortgages will be inevitable. It will mean less value for our Canadian dollar if we travel abroad. It will mean higher taxes and less money for personal spending. That in turn means business and industry cutbacks. People simply will not be able to buy new cars, new appliances, or new homes. As a result there will be fewer jobs. Everything is all related, all down the road. I say every Canadian suffers as a result of these deficits.
The question obviously is why do we have them? I must say to you, Sir, that from today's perspective it is a great deal easier to explain how they came about than why they came about. Spending at all levels of government in Canada has been rising since the end of World War II, partly at least in response to increased public demand for more government aid and more government services. Until the early 1970s growth in government spending was matched by rising government revenue: a very logical and simplistic balance existed. As people wanted more services and wanted more government aid, we were able to match that at all levels of government because rising government revenues balanced and matched those expenditures.
Then in the early 1970s governments seemed to become concerned about raising taxes. However, they also started spending at an even greater rate, especially the federal Government. To make up for this imbalance, governments, especially the federal Government, began borrowing against the future through deficit financing. That has resulted in the Government's asking the Parliament of Canada today to pass a borrowing Bill which, as I say, is the largest in Canadian history.
In 1976 the accumulated federal Government debt since Confederation-a time period which encompasses two world wars with vast expenditures on armies and armaments- totalled $22 billion. Now, as the last Budget indicated, our federal deficit is increasing yearly by more than what was our 109-year total just eight years ago. Last year the federal Government alone borrowed more than $26 billion. Ottawa's total debt now exceeds $130 billion. Mr. Speaker, that means you and I are $5,200 in debt; $5,200 for every man, woman and child in the country. According to the Budget forecast, $800 will be added to that debt each year for each and every one of us. Incidentally, when those of us who live in the Province of Ontario add on the debt of the Ontario Government-and I am sure it is roughly the same for every provincial government across the country-we have a debt of about $8,000. Every resident of the Province of Ontario, thanks to the combined governmental debt load of both the province and the federal Government, is now about $8,000 in debt and it is getting heavier by $1,100 every year.
I was very interested to read just recently that the Chairman of the Toronto-Dominion Bank, for instance, pointed out that if the parents of a child born today started borrowing in that child's name at the same rate of $1,100 per year, by the time the child was 25 years of age he or she would be in hock for
March 15, 1984

almost $120,000. That is a great deal of money as far as the average citizen is concerned. Obviously no responsible parent would think of doing that. It is almost inconceivable, yet that is exactly what is being done to our children and their children right now through government deficit financing and the imposition of a government Bill borrowing to the extent we are being asked to authorize today.
What is the answer? There is no easy one, but I think we have to start looking at it a darn sight harder than we have in the past. Otherwise we will awaken one day to find that we have a major economic collapse on our hands. Obviously part of the problem is that government has grown too large and has become too fat in the process. We must look at it closely to determine whether we really need and can afford all those offices, all those employees, all those bureaucrats, all those expensive Crown corporations and all the services they provide. We have to put it bluntly to our constituents: if we want to keep all these services, then we will have to start paying for them through much higher taxes. It is as simple as that.
If the question is put fairly to these people, I suggest they will realize that we have to go the other route. Obviously there is some fear that reducing the deficit must mean a cutback in the universal social welfare system of which Canada is so proud, such things as the family allowance and the old age pension. In fact, they are a very small part of the problem. Recent calculations show that if old age pensions and family allowances were restricted to families with less than $30,000 annual incomes, the savings would only be about $1 billion. That is a tiny proportion of next year's projected $30 billion federal deficit. This is why we as a Party and our Leader last week reaffirmed that we were certainly committed to reducing the federal deficit. Universality of social programs and opposition to any form of means test is a cornerstone of this Party's political philosophy in any event.
This is the only vehicle I have as a Member of the House to protest deeply the Government's mismanagement of the economy over the whole time it has been in office. This is why I speak today and voice my opposition to the horrendous Bill before us.

Yes, to Canadair-and to the very large corporations which have the ear of government, whether it is the Liberal Government in Ottawa or the Conservative Government in provinces like Ontario. Also it will go to land speculation which will make land more expensive without actually increasing its value. It will go to mergers and take-overs which have already destroyed many thousands of jobs. It will go to foreign investment in the way of tax gifts to those projects. Generally speaking, those projects do not create any more new jobs. They may create a few jobs by destroying more jobs, but the net result is that they do not create any new jobs. What the country needs above all is a restoration of employment and the prospect of full employment for everyone who is willing and able to work.
A year ago the Roman Catholic bishops spoke on this point and advocated two principles which the borrowing Bill opposes. One principle was the preference for the poor. The principle was that if we fulfilled the needs of the poor, the rich would also have their needs fulfilled. That is the opposite of the trickle-down theory espoused by the federal Government and by most provincial governments. The trickle-down theory holds that if we take taxes from poor people and give them to the rich, then some day some of that money will be returned to the poor people from whom it was taken in the first place. Most poor people do not think they will live long enough to see that day.
The second principle was the priority of labour over capital. Obviously the bishops do not mean by "labour" the Canadian Labour Congress or by "capital" the Canadian Manufacturers Association. They were talking about a basic fact of human life, namely that live, present labour uses past or dead labour. The goods we produced yesterday, a year ago or a century ago, whether they be railroads, trucks, factory buildings, electrical power, food or whatever, are dead labour. They are capital. They are intended to be used in the service of live labour, which is the new work we will do today. That is how I understand the teaching of the Roman Catholic bishops. They are saying that today's work must take priority over the results of yesterday's work, not the other way around.
This Bill ignores that principle. It suggests the Government should have more billions of dollars to hand out in the way it has been handing them out; that is, giving to people who simply increase the dollar value of yesterday's work. They will argue about who is going to be the president of the company that will control that capital. No new jobs will be created with that $29.5 billion.
It would be possible to support this borrowing Bill if the Government would reverse that principle. I am certain that support could be found in this corner of the House. I cannot speak so confidently for the moss-backs to my extreme right, but I hope that support will be found across the way. If the order were reversed, the working men and women in Canada would support it.

March 15, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
One-fifth of the workforce in Canada is either completely unemployed or severely under-employed. That is our greatest unused resource. If we had 25 per cent more people working, that one-fifth, that is 25 per cent more than now, working at their best, we could wipe out a $29.5 billion debt in very short order. We would cure many other troubles as well. It would be worth borrowing the $29.5 billion if the Government would apply it in that way. The Government would have to reform the tax laws so that over half of it would not be given to corporations. Instead, they could institute a program that would eliminate unemployment in a short while by suggesting that each worker should work four days a week and be paid the fifth day to study, train or improve himself or herself for the new challenges in the workforce that are in front of us right now.
We say we need a workforce capable of doing something more than dull manual labour or pen-pushing. That is true. We need a workforce capable of handling the new challenges of modern technology. The way to do that is to enable not just a small, select few to study, not just those who have been forced out of active work by layoffs to study and not just those who have been discouraged by years of unemployment. They should have the opportunity to study until they are ready to be employed again when the country is ready to use them.
If this $29.5 billion were used to enable all workers-men, women, youth, middle-aged and older workers-to study one-fifth of their time and also include the one-fifth unemployed and under-employed in the active workforce, we would not only save close to $15 billion in unemployment insurance but save another large amount in welfare. We would restore our educational system which is falling into ruin through cutbacks if we applied this $29 billion in that way. Best of all, we would mobilize the workforce with a kind of enthusiasm that has not been seen since World War II. We have not had a labour shortage in Canada since World War II. We should have such a problem again!
With a program such as this, we would put a hopeful prospect in front of all Canada's workers, both those who are working and those who are not. We would give them something to look forward to by way of sharing in active terms as workers in the growth of this country. I hope that an idea like this will be taken seriously by those on the Government benches, to the extent that they will seriously want to reconstruct Canada, to rebuild our economy. The resource we have to use is the one-fifth of our workforce that is unemployed or under-employed. The best place to use the $29 billion is in putting those people immediately to work.

Sixth, improved accounting procedures and practices for Crown corporations conforming to principles and practices accepted in the private sector.

One of our American colleagues said that yes, he himself was a new hopeful; he was younger than Senator Hart, he had been in the House for fewer years than Senator Hart, he had some new ideas since breakfast and he may even have had some new ideas since lunch. He would be prepared, if he could just think about those ideas long enough, to articulate them and present them to us as a hopeful leader of his Party.
That situation reminds me of the situation of the unfortunate "Minister of oink oink", who truly believes that a man of his tattered reputation can possibly be taken seriously by the Canadian electorate, particularly by those who live in ridings which were deprived of his particular brand of porkbarreling.

As a new Member of Parliament I should like to take a few moments to describe my feelings about this $29.5 billion. In 1968 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was chosen to lead the Liberal Party, he said there would be a just society for all Canadians. Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to you that the problems in this country will not be bilingualism or regional distribution; the problem in this country is the pork-barreling that is going on.
Before being elected as a Member of this House, Mr. Speaker, I thought it would be an honour to have the opportunity to represent the riding of Timiskaming and take part in the history of Canada as one of the 282 Members of Parliament. Before my election to this House I was told, and I believed, that as long as one was honest and sincere and worked hard for his constituents, it would be for the betterment of the country. March 15, 1984

Mr. Speaker, it just delays matters and it does not give me any of the funding that has been made available to elected Members.
The last Budget did nothing to help the unemployed of this country, Mr. Speaker. In this country there are mines, sawmills, and industries in which men and women have worked 20 or 25 years and at the age of 45, 50 or 60 have found themselves out of work. Today there is nothing for them. Was this addressed in the Budget? No, it was not. Did the Budget address the question of financial assistance to the spouse of 50, 55 or 60 years of age who has lost her husband? No, it did not. Is this a just society, Mr. Speaker? I really believe that if we are going to work together the unemployed of this country should not be punished because they happen to have a democratic right to elect whom they please.
The people who are unemployed or on welfare, those who cannot find work, are being discriminated against because in a democratic election they decided to support the Conservative Party. Now they are being penalized for that. Hon. Members opposite should consider the position of these people. subsubtopic: TAX COURT OF CANADA-BACKLOG OF CASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, public attention focused on the operation of Revenue Canada has revealed auditing and assessing practices that have resulted in financial difficulty, even disaster, for many Canadian taxpayers. The disturbing element in many cases is that Revenue Canada's quest for money overrides fair application of the taxation rules.
In order to protect Canadian taxpayers from over-zealous and unfair tax collectors, it is essential that we have an effective and accessible appeal process. This process should involve independent officers who can apply impartial judgment to tax questions. In short, the tax appeal process must provide a judicial forum for settlement of tax disputes.
In 1983 Parliament created the Tax Court of Canada, presumably to guarantee fair treatment for Canadian taxpayers. The Government claimed that the Tax Court of Canada would provide easy and expense-free access for taxpayers who dispute tax assessments made by Revenue Canada. It is, therefore, disturbing to discover this newly constituted tax court is already jammed with a backlog of cases, which will create unreasonable delays in processing cases. Justice delayed is justice denied, especially when those taxed must pay in advance.
If the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) wants to be fair to Canadian taxpayers, he will act immediately to expedite income tax appeals and ensure that the Tax Court of Canada has adequate personnel and resources to carry out its parliamentary mandate.

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, I recently visited the Sioux Valley School which is operated by the Sioux Valley Indian Band in my constituency. On that day the students were unable to attend classes because the sewage system had backed up. There were other problems. The school is actually a cluster of small buildings, and the result is a fragmented student population. As well, there are no gymnasium facilities to speak of, and one building is a health and safety hazard.
Despite these conditions, in the five years since the Sioux Valley Indian Band assumed responsiblity for operating the school, the student population has grown, attendance has improved, and students who had once dropped out of offreserve schools have now returned to Sioux Valley to finish their education. Clearly this band has risen to the challenge of preparing for self government.
It is ironic, therefore, that the federal Government is discouraging the band's efforts. Despite repeated pleas by the band for a new school with decent facilities, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has refused to construct one until at least 1987, and very possibly much later. The band has offered to take out a loan to finance the construction, but it needs a loan guarantee from the federal Government, and that has not been forthcoming. The Sioux Valley school, therefore, joins a growing backlog of capital projects in Indian education.
Like numerous other Indian bands, the Sioux Valley band has demonstrated that it is capable of meeting its own commitment to education. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development should hold up its end of the bargain.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION-ANNOUNCED CLOSURE OF VANCOUVER OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Transport Commission's Air Transport Committee office in Vancouver is being forced to close in April. This office, which enforces CTC air regulations affecting the licensing of air carriers, is closing because Treasury Board refuses to grant one and one-half more person years. Only five field officers cover our entire nation. Yet other sectors receive billions of dollars. The best way to promote air industry is to ensure safety.
When the Vancouver office closes, the Edmonton field office will have to cover B.C., Alberta, Yukon, and the Northwest Territories. B.C. is experiencing the fastest growth in Canada in the number of new air carriers. Small carriers servicing the resource industries are sprouting up all over B.C. and the Yukon. Yet the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) shuts the Vancouver office, and keeps the Winnipeg office open despite the negligible growth in Manitoba.
Effective licensing enforcement is crucial for air safety. The air industry is a very exacting and technical industry. The terrain in B.C. and the Yukon is among the most treacherous in the flying world, Mr. Speaker. For the safety of all Canadians, all tourists, and everyone flying in B.C. and the Yukon, I urge the Minister of Transport not to close the Vancouver office, to remain within his budget Estimates, and to consider alternatives other than safety.

import. That will also be passed on to the consumer and will mean higher costs of living for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have difficulty understanding that the Minister actually believes all of what he has just said. He did not say it with his usual elan.
1980 ELECTION PROMISE

Mr. Speaker, in reply to this question, perhaps I may refer my hon. colleague to what was said in the House on Monday, March 12 of this year. Unfortunately, the Hon. Member was not in the House when we discussed the entire matter of interest rates and the value of the dollar. My reply is therefore the one given on page 1981 of the Hansard, where I said:
Neither the Bank of Canada nor I wish to see a substantial devaluation of the Canadian dollar with the inflation rate consequences that would follow, and which would ultimately produce higher interest rates as well. At the same time neither would we wish to see a sharp rise in interest rates, particularly at this stage of the recovery. The policy which has been followed, therefore, has been one of moderating movements, both in the exchange rate and in interest rates. My objective is to ensure that the significant and hard won gains in reducing inflation over the past two years are preserved and the momentum of our recovery is maintained.

RESIGNATION OF MEMBER FOR SCARBOROUGH EAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great regret and a deep sense of personal loss that I have today tendered my resignation as the Member of Parliament for Scarborough East. It is my unshakeable belief that my constituents are entitled to the best possible representation without any shadow of doubt cast on the integrity of their Member of Parliament. The verdict in my tax trial has created a doubt as to my ability vigorously and honourably to represent my constituents. If I cannot serve them honourably, I will not serve at all.
However, let there be no doubt in anyone's mind. I believe that this judgment is wrong. My company, my family and I are innocent and I believe that was proven by the evidence which was presented at the trial. Accordingly, I have instructed my counsel to commence appeal proceedings immediately. I only wish that this appeal could be heard well before the coming election. Without that certainty, I cannot in all fairness allow my personal situation to impair the choices of my
March 15, 1984

constituents in the crucial issues which they and all Canadians must judge in the next election. Similarly, I cannot and will not allow this issue to in any way reflect badly upon the great Party and the outstanding Leader which I have been so privileged to serve.
The costs of defending my company's good name, measured both in dollars and in personal anguish to the members of my family, have been enormous. They have caused me to understand in all too graphic terms the staggering burden imposed on the taxpayers of the country in meeting both the absurd complexities of the Canadian tax system and the overwhelming power of Revenue Canada. In spite of these burdens, I intend to pursue this matter to clear the good name of my business, my family and myself. To this end I am therefore privileged that Mr. John J. Robinette, Q.C., has agreed to act as counsel on my appeal, furthering the fine work already done by Messrs. Stikeman, Elliott.
I cannot adequately express my gratitude for the steadfast support which I have received from so many of my constituents irrespective of their political affiliation throughout this entire ordeal. It has been a privilege and an honour to have served them. I thank them from the bottom of my heart and hope that I have met their expectations in the performance of that service. Finally, I am deeply indebted to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) and to every member of the Progressive Conservative caucus for their undiminished support and friendship.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. MacLaren that Bill C-21, an Act to provide borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
For various reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to Bill C-21 to provide borrowing authority. Since the beginning of this debate, I have heard my colleagues opposite make every kind of unwarranted accusations. I should think that the basic question in this whole debate is whether the Budget will foster the economic recovery. It all depends on the political approach or doctrine which one may have or uphold in this House, and that is what we have been hearing since the beginning. Some Conservatives whom I will not mention, even though I made a note of their riding-my time being limited, I do not intend to single out every unwarranted allegation that has been made-have tried to isolate certain votes, one in particular which this Government adopted to promote investment in high technology, de Havilland and Canadair in this case. However, they remained silent about de Havilland when the Government was blamed for its approach to the future of Canadair. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in answering a question today, we have to decide whether technology will stay here or be exported to other countries such as the United States.
Mr. Speaker, a number of countries in the world-France, England, Belgium and the United States among others-have developed their aeronautical industry through defence budget appropriations. If we in Canada want to support our aeronautical industry, we will have to spend money and foot the bills. When it was decided to take over de Havilland and Canadair from the private sector in 1975-76 to secure the future of our aircraft industry, I remember very well that
Borrowing Authority Act
Canadair had 825 employees. Eventually, Canadair ended up with a labour force of 8,000 in that field of high technology.
That is the challenge which the Liberal Government agreed to face in that highly technical field, so as to offer job opportunities to young Canadians now attending school.
Last March 8 in the House, I stressed the importance of developing that high technology sector. In Montreal alone, 12,310 CEGEP graduates of 1982 and 1983 invaded the labour market to seek employment in engineering and science. There are seven engineering schools which specialize in research and have created 2,110 graduates in 1982-83. It is for them that we want to promote high technology, Mr. Speaker.
I was proud to hear the Prime Minister and the President of the Treasury Board say today that, of course, it is imperative to change the structure of Canadair. When he appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs on March 13, the Minister responsible, Senator Jack Austin, spoke of our awareness to make some changes in Canadair. Those changes were explained when the Budget was under consideration. We know that Canadair management was wont to see everything through rose-coloured glasses. Not that we did not try to tell them! They had an overly optimistic outlook on marketability and closed their eyes on obvious operational problems. Even their accountants were riding on cloud nine. In addition, they tried to make the Government look on the bright side, while at the same time glossing over their difficulties. The company was overstaffed and the responsibilities of management were not clear cut. That is why the Canada Development Investment Corporation made it a priority to bring the company back to earth and reduce its operational expenditures. As a result of those measures, the deficit went from $145,100,000 in 1982 down to $83 million in 1983. So, there were two possibilities: either take the approach of the Progressive Conservatives and bail out, or adopt the Liberal philosophy, see what could be done to improve management and maintain jobs in the field of technology. Mr. Speaker, I have here an article published in the Montreal Gazette of February 20 and written by Mr. Nick Auf der Maur. It is a biography of the Leader of the Opposition and it says:
Killing of Arrow Still Hurts Today
Twenty-five years ago today, at 11 a.m.. Prime Minister John Diefenbaker got up in the House of Commons to announce a momentous decision that still lives with us.
He cancelled the Avro Arrow program, the CF-105 fighter-interceptor that aviation experts say would still be one of the best aircraft in the world if it were flying today.
Arguably, it was a decision that adversely affected Canada's industrial capacity, and wreaked such havoc on our aerospace industries that they still haven't fully recovered.
That day, Feb. 20, 1959, is still known as Black Friday in the industry.

March 15, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
That day, 22,000 Canadians were thrown out of work-14,000 at the A.V. Roe and Orenda engine plants in the Toronto region, the rest from suppliers mostly in the Montreal area.
And an estimated $475 million in development and production costs were simply poured down that drain. (That was roughly the same cost as the St. Lawrence Seaway, built in about the same period, or an estimated $3 billion in today's terms.)

It is exactly the same attitude Progressive Conservatives are taking twenty-five years later. They would rather get rid of the problem instead of coping with it. We on the Government side are prepared to support the aerospace industry, and as far as Quebecers are concerned, the questions that have been asked since the beginning of the debate on this Bill are entirely unacceptable. The Progressive Conservatives are denying Quebecers an opportunity to take part in the expansion of our high technology industries. That is the difference between our Liberal philosophy and the philosophy of the Progressive Conservatives. To hear them talk, we ought to close the airport at Mirabel. The Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) has spoken many times here in the House, and the leadership candidate, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), said today that Canadair should be shut down! What will be left for Quebecers with a Progressive Conservative Government and a balance-the-Budget philosophy? Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of attitude, and when I look at the investments the Government of Canada has made in the Province of Quebec in the last few months, and I am referring to federal investments in major industries in the Montreal area, it really confirms that we have a different approach, especially when we look at the Budget, which has earmarked $996 million for the construction of patrol frigates, $368 million for research and development at Pratt & Whitney . .. That is the kind of funding Parliament is being asked to approve to provide various departments with the money they need and to continue the economic recovery process in Canada. I could go on, Mr. Speaker: $165 million for the Bell Helicopter project; $30 million for the agro-food research centre; $ 15 million for the office automation research centre in Laval; $10 million for the robotics centre at the Lionel-Groulx CEGEP; and I could go on and on Mr. Speaker. We have $2,843 billion that will be spent by the Liberal Government on developing the high-tech industry in the Province of Quebec. As for the attitude of the Progressive Conservatives who spoke in the House and who regularly question the Government about developments at Canadair, twenty-five years ago that very same group buried the Arrow when Mr. Diefenbaker was Prime Minister. My constituents sometimes ask me what borrowing authority Bills do. I explain to them that Governments all require parliamentary authority to borrow new money. First, people want to know how much money these eight requests add up to. Telling them that the Government has forced us to borrow $102.85 billion since 1980 begs another question. The answer is that Government spending is out of control.
Since 1968, Government spending has increased approximately 668 per cent. Since 1980 alone, it has risen by 97 per cent to the point where it is now 25 per cent of our gross national product. What has this done to our requirement to borrow? Well, in 1984, according to the estimates, we will spend 21.5 per cent of Canadians' tax dollars on servicing the national debt. In the year just before the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his gang of spenders over there took over, the Government was spending only 11.6 per cent of taxes on paying off that debt. This has caused us to borrow over $100 billion in the last four years. This Government has thrown money at all its problems rather than taking the time to look for real solutions. By doing so, the Government has increased

Government spending from just over $12 billion in 1968-69 to slightly over $100 billion in 1983-84, all at the expense of the taxpayer.
When I explain this to my constituents they cannot understand how little regard the Government has for their hard earned tax dollars. I try to explain the situation to them. Imagine that the Government is a bank, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) is the bank president and Parliament is its board of directors. On this board of directors, the president has a majority of the votes on his side. Each of the eight times in the last four years the Government has needed money, the bank president has asked the board to give him another loan. As loyal friends of the president the majority of the directors, without question, agreed to do so. However, the minority of directors did ask questions, and twice succeeded in reducing the amount of the loan slightly. Because the board, in this case Parliament, was loaded with unswerving and unquestioning followers of the president-the Minister of Finance-the loans were granted. This was done irrespective of the financial position of the loan requestor, the Government, or of the interests of its owners, the people of Canada.
I would like Hon. Members sitting over there on the Government benches to put themselves in the position of the bank manager of one of their local banks. If any company came to you today and made a request to borrow $29 billion, what questions would you ask? First, you would ask for the company's financial position as of its last fiscal year. If that company told you that its deficit last year was about $31.5 billion, I think you would then ask what their net position was at the end of last year. A response giving a net debt of over $150 billion would not, I am sure, dispose you towards lending further funds to that company. If you asked a company what it expects its profit to be over the next five years, as Revenue Canada does of some farmers, and the company told you that it expected its yearly deficit to remain nearly constant and its net debt to almost double, would you not write them off as a bad credit risk, as does Revenue Canada?
I have been through this kind of an ordeal with constituents of mine who were applying for loans through the Farm Credit Corporation and through the Industrial and Regional Development Program. Neither of these institutions would touch a company or an individual in this type of financial position. On a few occasions they have told companies that they must change their management structure, as they obviously were not being run correctly, before they would even talk to them about Government loans.

Let me use the example of an unemployed worker. There is a major difference between that unemployed worker borrowing a substantial amount in order to go to Hawaii for a vacation and borrowing to purchase a car so that he can get to a nearby town to find employment. There is a big difference between this Government's borrowing money so that it can give $8 billion over the next few years to oil companies that will be drilling on Canada Lands, whether or not they drill dry holes, and conversely borrowing money to be used for labour-intensive projects which would help restore our economy to a sound footing, putting people back to work and ending some of the misery of unemployment.
Our Party would be much more open to this Bill if the Government were serious about the major problems affecting Canada today, but we see no indication of that. Where is the Government's commitment to reverse the loss of jobs and the drain this creates on the total economy? Victoria, B.C., in the southern part of my constituency, now has the second highest level of unemployment in Canada. People in that community are suffering deeply from the knock-out punch of the punitive attitude of the provincial Social Credit Government and the neglect of the federal Government. While a great deal of attention has been focused on the punishing attitude of the provincial government and the neglect of the federal Government, the attitude and drift it has taken toward basic resource industries such as forestry and the fisheries is, in the long run, almost as disastrous as the punishing attitude of the Socreds.
Another area of Government neglect about which I would like to speak briefly is the whole area of Indian Affairs. Last week Canadians witnessed the last minute conversion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to at least the rhetoric of aboriginal self-government. There was some surprise when the provinces did not buy this rhetoric as it was presented to them.
If we look at the Prime Minister's proposal, we see that it lacked any real commitment to the aboriginal people. We see that the Government's response to the report of the Special Committee on Indian Self-Government lacked any specific economic commitment to the Indian people. Indian self-government without economic commitment to back it up will be nothing more than a comic opera, a meaningless charade.
Let us look at housing on Indian reserves. Housing is connected to the concomitant problems of sewer and water. These are woefully inadequate on reserves from one end of Canada to another. We can point to some outstanding examples where housing, water and sewage systems are good, but by and large the housing situation across Canada is woefully inadequate. It is tied in with the terrible standard of health
Borrowing Authority Act
that Indian people have to face, the high drop-out rate of Indian children at shcool, unemployment and the loss of culture. When people do not have adequate housing and an adequate infrastructure in their communities, all of these other things tend to go by the board as well.
Across Canada right now, there is the phenomenon of Indian people being forced off the reserves and away from their home communities into the crowded ghettos of large cities. Once those Indians are in the ghettos, the federal Government thinks it is able to wash its hands of them and no longer provides them with basic services. For example, educational services to off-reserve Indian people were terminated last year. Indian people find themselves forced into a welfare system.
This year, the Department of Indian Affairs is saying that it will not be able to fund training programs for the urban training centre in Vancouver. Last December, some attention was directed to the case of Joyce and Birdie Canton, an Indian couple from the Wabigoon Reserve in northwestern Ontario who moved to the City of Winnipeg because their home on the reserve was condemned for health reasons. However, I think it is important to remember that a couple like the Cantons are not the exception to the rule. Rather, they were exceptional only because of the fact that they received a certain amount of media attention because they refused to submit quietly to the indignity of bad housing and welfare when they did not want to do so and should not expect to have to do so.
In 1979, it was estimated that the Indian people across Canada had a housing shortage with a backlog of some 13,000 units. Five years later, our best guess is that there are still some 10,000 housing units urgently needed on Indian reserves.

Mr. Speaker, standing in the Chamber today, I am reminded of the day that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) called Members of Parliament nobodies. Far too often, when out in our ridings around the country, we tend to think that what happens in the Chamber of the House of Commons is irrelevant to the day-to-day lives of the people. Today, Mr. Speaker, we are looking at the largest borrowing Bill in Canadian history. We can predict that members of the Liberal Party of Canada will stand up in the Chamber and vote for it. Will that affect the lives of individual ordinary Canadians?
On a day-to-day basis this week we have watched the value of the Canadian dollar drop. During the auction for Treasury notes today, interest rates went up better than one half of 1 per cent. Anyone who bought a home this morning or who yesterday put in his offer to buy, did the paperwork necessary to receive a mortgage, but now finds that he is having his pocketbook tapped this afternoon. One half of 1 per cent on a $50,000 mortgage amounts to extra payments of better than $20 a month of after-tax income out of a wage earner's pocket. If that mortgage is $100,000, one half of 1 per cent amounts to an extra $40 a month. That is $40 a month that people cannot use for food, clothing, entertainment and education.
This situation has been caused by a further four years on top of 11 years of economic mismanagment. It is hurting the country. It is costing the country jobs. It is costing the people anxiety and putting more people in hospitals. How did such a situation come about? Government Members, including all the leadership candidates, are asking Members of the House of Commons to give them permission to borrow $29,550 million. That is a sum so staggering that it defies the imagination.
Let us put that amount in perspective, Mr. Speaker. There are 24 million Canadians, and some of them are in the fortunate position of being able to save money either by putting it in banks or in a variety of money certificates. The amount of money the Government wants to borrow from those who save is 91 per cent of all the money that will be saved in the country this year. This government borrowing Bill does not even include the amounts to be borrowed by Crown corporations, which are an extension of Government.
If the Government will borrow 91 cents out of every dollar that every Canadian saves, that leaves only nine cents for the rest of us to borrow for the purchase of a car or a home. Because of this, what happens to the interest rates, Mr. Speaker? This Bill has not yet been passed, is not yet law, and the borrowing has not even begun. We are only at the beginning stages of this Bill, and already interest rates are up one half of 1 per cent. Perhaps they will rise another 1 per cent, 1.5 per cent or 2 per cent. Everyone who borrows money in the ocuntry will have to pay that extra amount.
Pensioners in the country who are on fixed incomes will have to pay more for the food they eat because the costs run down throughout the entire economy. Rents will go up and the cost of medical supplies will go up as well. If any Member of this Chamber thinks that what we do here does not affect ordinary Canadians, he is pulling the wool over his eyes. This is the largest borrowing Bill in Canadian history.
This year the Government plans to spend almost twice as much as it planned to spend the day it was elected. In four years it has almost doubled its expenditures and it has more than doubled the amount of money it borrows. People do not like high interest rates. They complain that their business went bankrupt because they could not afford those rates, that they had to turn their home back to the mortgage company because they could not pay the interest, or that the finance company repossessed their car. They should hold every single Member of the Liberal Party of Canada accountable because they support Government mismanagement year after year after year. It is the Government's willingness to borrow year after year after year that is causing the problem. Some may say that the blame lies with the Cabinet, but that is not so. Members of this Chamber vote for these measures and so it is the job of government backbenchers and opposition Parties to hold the Cabinet accountable and put some common sense into the legislation. When government backbenchers do not do that job, then the voters of the country have a job to do, and that is, to kick each and every one of them out of this Chamber so that they never have an opportunity to do this sort of thing again.
When I was elected almost five years ago, 17 cents out of every tax dollar went to pay interest on the public debt and 83 cents was left for health care, unemployment insurance and so on. Now, not quite five years later, 31 cents out of every tax dollar goes to pay interest on the public debt. That leaves 69 cents instead of 83 cents to go into health care, pensions, and
March 15, 1984

all the things people expect the Government to provide. That is a tragedy, Mr. Speaker.
There are 1.5 million people unemployed. Young people want to go to university, but governments are cutting back on funding for universities. People want to go to hospital and cannot because beds are not available. The reason behind all this is the economic mismanagement of the Liberal Party of Canada, and it has gone on far too long and hurts too many people.
The story must be told and the lessons learned, Mr. Speaker.
I urge Canadians, wherever they live, to take a good, hard look at the behaviour of their politicians and what they say they believe in and compare it to what they do in this Chamber. What they do is to vote to support that mismanagement and the Cabinet. Unless Members across the way have a change of heart and start to behave differently, Canadians have an obligation to turf each and every one of them out, not only in this election but for the rest of the elections in this century. That is the obligation of Canadian voters.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I participate in the debate on Bill C-21 with the faint flicker of hope that the government Members may exercise their ancient but rather atrophied power to bring some sense to the Government's spending policies. Bill C-21 is an abomination. It lays an immense burden on the people of Canada today and on future generations. That is spelled out in the rather brief piece of legislation which provides for the Government to borrow $29.55 billion or, as my colleague has just put it, twenty-nine and a half thousand million dollars. That tidy sum for a profligate and spendthrift administration exceeds by $4 billion the entire financial requirements of the Government for a full fiscal year. That is not the full fiscal year that we are now in but the full fiscal year to come. That projection of the requirement was announced in the House one month ago today. Now the Government brings in a Bill asking for $29.55 billion to see it through the entire fiscal year beginning April 1.
I pause here to note that it is rather strange that there existed on February 29 a full $5 billion in unused borrowing authority, and I asked myself why it is so essential that today, before the fiscal year begins, the Government should ask Parliament for authority to spend the entire financial requirement as projected in the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) well in advance of the period yet to begin.
It occurs to me that it might be convenient if the House were no longer required by the Government of the day-if it might be sent into recess while those seeking the hollow grail of leadership of the Liberal Party were permitted to travel the country pursuing their own personal goals. It would also be convenient if the House were muted in its discussion in this place of the waste and extravagance undertaken by the Government. In place of the legitimate criticism that is levelled in the House we might have an expensive advertising campaign initiated by the Government to tell the people of Canada that the days of wine and roses has returned. The contrary is the truth, Mr. Speaker.
Borrowing Authority Act
Yesterday, as a consequence of a meeting of a committee of this House, we heard that the Government had decided to pump an additional $310 million into Canadair. That is in addition to the $1.4 billion that had been accumulated as a consequence of the guarantees provided to that corporation- guarantees of the Government of Canada over the years and written off, assumed by the Government of Canada in 1983. Senator Austin has told the country that the project undertaken by that company will succeed and that it will be profitable.
I wonder what would have happened to the Ford Motor Company if the chairman of the board had said that they would sell Edsels and that Edsels would be profitable.
The problem with the Government and the Crown corporations that it sustains is that there is no relationship between reality and its goals. It is appropriate to think positively and it is wise and prudent to endeavour to achieve the best we can with the instruments that have been given to us. It is foolhardy, however, to pursue goals which result in the further wasting of the finances of the people of Canada. These funds are not the Government's funds. They are the funds of the people of this nation. The people sitting in this House as Members of Parliament have an obligation to the people whom they represent to administer their financial affairs astutely. It is for that purpose that my colleagues and I stand here in our places and endeavour to persuade members of the government Party to come to their senses. Just a smattering of good judgement exercised by them would stop this process.
What is the process with which we are currently involved? It is the borrowing of money, which has the effect of creating an opinion of the way in which this Government has performed, not only in the financial community of Canada but in the financial communities of the world. And what is the judgement of those who can reflect their judgement in a positive sense? As compared to other currencies, our currency is under attack. It is under attack because it is overvalued as a result of the Government of Canada reaching too far into the combined savings and assets of the people of this nation. The Government has shown internationally that it is unequipped to deal with the financial affairs of Canada.
The Minister of Finance stood in his place in the House and explained that interest rates, if they rise, are beyond the control of this Government because interest rates in the United States are increasing. Interest rates will rise, Mr. Speaker, so long as the Government and the Minister of Finance intervene with the Bank of Canada, as they do regularly. The Government, in fact, instructs the Bank of Canada on what price should be paid at the Treasury bill auction every Thursday. We know what the effect of that was today, that is, 10.56 per cent. We know what the increase will signal to the financial community. It will signal that interest rates should also go up on commercial loans and on home mortgages. What will the effect of that be, Mr. Speaker? It will return this nation to the series of bankruptcies and home foreclosures and judicial sales of the assets of the people of this nation, from which we hoped we might extricate ourselves, relying on the financial recovery

of the United States. That will not occur if this Government persists with the spending practices which it has unveiled in Bill C-21.
I urge Hon. Members of the House, if they are concerned about their constituents and about the welfare of Canadians in general, if they really hope to create employment through the resurrection of a stable, profitable business community, and if they hope to keep people who have acquired homes in those homes, to reflect upon the lack of wisdom which is embodied in Bill C-21.
